subject: Physics
text: A transverse wave on a string is described by $y = 3\sin(36t + 0.018x + \pi/4)$. Where $x, y$ are in $\text{cm}$ and $t$ in seconds. The least distance between the two successive crests in the wave is _______ $\text{cm}$. (Nearest integer) ($\pi = 3.14$)
solution:
Least distance between successive crest = $\lambda$
$y = A\sin(\omega t + kx + \phi)$, $\omega = 2\pi f$ & $k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$
& $y = A\sin(36t + 0.018x + \pi/4)$
$$\Rightarrow k = 0.018\text{ cm}^{-1} \Rightarrow \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} = 0.018$$
$$\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{0.018} = \frac{2 \times 3.14}{18 \times 10^{-3}}\text{ cm} = 348.88\text{ cm} \approx 349\text{ cm} \text{ (nearest integer)}$$

subject: Physics
text: A series LCR circuit with $R = 20\,\Omega$, $L = 1.6\text{ H}$ and $C = 40\;\mu\text{F}$ is connected to a variable frequency a.c. source. The inductive reactance at resonant frequency is ___ $\Omega$.
solution: For resonance\n$$\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1.6 \times 40 \times 10^{-6}}} = \frac{10^3}{8} = 125$$\n$$X_L = \omega L = 125 \times 1.6 = 200\;\Omega$$

subject: Physics
text:
The energy released when $\frac{7}{17.13}\text{ kg}$ of ${}_3^7\text{Li}$ is converted into ${}_2^4\text{He}$ by proton bombardment is $\alpha \times 10^{32}\text{ eV}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______ (Nearest integer)
(Mass of ${}_3^7\text{Li} = 7.0183\text{ u}$, mass of ${}_2^4\text{He} = 4.004\text{ u}$, mass of proton = $1.008\text{ u}$ and $1\text{ u} = 931\text{ MeV/c}^2$ and Avogadro number = $6.0 \times 10^{23}$)
solution:
Reaction: ${}_3^7\text{Li} + {}_1^1\text{P} \to 2{}_2^4\text{He}$
Mass defect $\Delta m = (7.0183 + 1.008) - 2(4.004) = 0.0183\text{ u}$
Number of moles of $\text{Li} = \frac{7}{17.13} \times \frac{10^3}{7} = \frac{10^3}{17.13}$
Number of molecules = $\frac{10^3}{17.13} \times 6 \times 10^{23}$
Total energy released:
$$E_{\text{Total}} = 0.0183 \times 931 \times \frac{6}{17.13} \times 10^{32}$$
$$\approx 6 \times 10^{32}$$
$$\alpha = 6$$

subject: Physics
text: A moving coil of galvanometer when shunted with $2\Omega$ resistance gives a full scale deflection for a current of $500\text{ mA}$. When a resistance of $470\Omega$ is connected in series it gives a full scale deflection for $10\text{ V}$ potential applied on it. The value of resistance of galvanometer coil is \underline{\hspace{1cm}} $\Omega$.
solution:
Given current $i = 500\text{ mA} = 0.5\text{ A} = \frac{1}{2}\text{ A}$
Shunt resistance $S = 2\Omega$
Using shunt formula: $i_g R_g = (i - i_g)S$
$i_g R_g = 2\left(\frac{1}{2} - i_g\right) \implies i_g = \frac{1}{R_g + 2}$
For the series combination with $R = 470\Omega$ and total voltage $10\text{ V}$:
$10 = (R_g + 470)i_g$
$10 = \frac{R_g + 470}{R_g + 2}$
$10R_g + 20 = R_g + 470$
$9R_g = 450 \implies R_g = 50\Omega$

subject: Physics
text: A $5\text{ mg}$ particle carrying a charge of $5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$ is moving with velocity of $(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{k}) \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}$ in a region having magnetic field $\vec{B} = 0.1\hat{k}\text{ Wb/m}^2$. It moves a distance of $\alpha$ meter along $\hat{k}$ when it completes $5$ revolutions. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
solution: $5 \left( \frac{2\pi m}{qB} \right) v \Rightarrow \frac{5 \times 2 \times \pi \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{-2}}{5 \pi \times 10^{-6} \times 0.1} = 2\text{ m}$

subject: Physics
text: 10 mole of oxygen is heated at constant volume from $30^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$. The change in the internal energy of the gas is $\qquad$ cal. (The molecular specific heat of oxygen at constant pressure, $C_p = 7 \text{ cal./mol } ^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $R = 2 \text{ cal./mol } ^{\circ}\text{C}$.)
solution:
$\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T$
$= n(C_p - R)\Delta T$
$= 10(7 - 2)(40 - 30)$
$\Delta U = 500$

subject: Physics
text: In a Young's double slit experiment set up, the two slits are kept $0.4\text{ mm}$ apart and screen is placed at $1\text{ m}$ from slits. If a thin transparent sheet of thickness $20\text{ \mu m}$ is introduced in front of one of the slits then centre bring fringe shifts by $20\text{ mm}$ on the screen. The refractive index of transparent sheet is given by $\frac{\alpha}{10}$, where $\alpha$ is _______.
solution:
$y_{\text{shift}} = \frac{(\mu - 1)t \cdot D}{d}$
$20 \times 10^{-3} = \frac{(\mu - 1) \times 20 \times 10^{-6} \times 1}{0.4 \times 10^{-3}}$
$(\mu - 1) = 0.4$
$\mu = 1.4$
$\frac{\alpha}{10} = 1.4, \alpha = 14$

subject: Physics
text: A circular disc has radius $R_1$ and thickness $T_1$. Another circular disc made of the same material has radius $R_2$ and thickness $T_2$. If the moment of inertia of both discs are same and $\frac{R_1}{R_2} = 2$ then $\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{1}{\alpha}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _____.

subject: Physics
text:
A cylindrical conductor of length $2\text{ m}$ and area of cross-section $0.2\text{ mm}^2$ carries an electric current of $1.6\text{ A}$ when its ends are connected to a $2\text{ V}$ battery. Mobility of electrons in the conductor is $\alpha \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2/\text{V}\cdot\text{s}$. The value of $\alpha$ is :
(electron concentration = $5 \times 10^{28}/\text{m}^3$ and electron charge = $1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$)
solution:
$V_d = \mu E = \mu \times \frac{V}{\ell}$
$I = neAV_d$
$V_d = \frac{I}{neA}$
$\mu = \frac{I\ell}{NneA}$ (where $N$ is number density, here $n$)
$\mu = \frac{1.6 \times 3}{2 \times 5 \times 10^{26} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2 \times 10^{-7}}$ (Wait, using given values: $\ell = 2\text{ m}$, area $A = 0.2\text{ mm}^2 = 0.2 \times 10^{-6}\text{{ m}}^2$)
From solution snippet: $\mu = 1 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2/\text{V}\cdot\text{s}$
$\alpha = 1$

subject: Physics
text: In two separate Young's double-slit experimental set-ups, two monochromatic light sources of different wavelengths are used to get fringes of equal width. The ratios of the slit separations and that of the wavelengths of light used are $2 : 1$ and $1 : 2$ respectively. The corresponding ratio of the distances between the slits and the respective screens $(D_1 / D_2)$ is $\rule{2cm}{0.15mm}$.
solution:
$$\beta_1 = \beta_2$$
$$\frac{D_1 \lambda_1}{d_1} = \frac{D_2 \lambda_2}{d_2}$$
$$\frac{D_1}{D_2} = \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} \left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)$$
$$= 2 \times 2$$
$$\frac{D_1}{D_2} = 4$$

subject: Physics
text: Suppose there is a uniform circular disc of mass $\text{M kg}$ and radius $r\text{ m}$ shown in figure. The shaded regions are cut out from the disc. The moment of inertia of the remainder about the axis A of the disc is given by $\frac{x}{256} M r^2$. The value of $x$ is _______.
solution:
$M = \sigma \pi R^2$
$\sigma \pi R^2 = 16\text{ m}$
$m = \frac{\sigma \pi R^2}{16}$
$I_{\text{system}} = \frac{MR^2}{2} - 2 \left(\frac{mR^2}{2 \times 16} + \frac{9mR^2}{16}\right)$
$= \frac{MR^2}{2} - 2 \times \frac{19mR^2}{32}$
$= \frac{MR^2}{2} - \frac{19}{16} mR^2$
$= \frac{MR^2}{2} - \frac{19}{256} MR^2 \quad \text{becoz } m = \frac{M}{16}$
$= \frac{(128 - 19)(MR^2)}{256}$
$= \frac{109 MR^2}{256}$

subject: Physics
text: In the given figure the blocks A, B and C weigh $4\text{ kg}$, $6\text{ kg}$ and $8\text{ kg}$ respectively. The co-efficient of sliding friction between any two surfaces is $0.5$. The force $\vec{F}$ required to slide the block C with constant speed is ______ $\text{N}$. (Used $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
solution:
For $8\text{ kg}$ to move with constant velocity $F_{\text{net}} = 0$.

Frictional forces:
$f_1 = 50\text{ N}$ (between A and B)
$f_2 = 20\text{ N}$ (string tension or interface)
$f_3 = 90\text{ N}$ (between C and ground)

$F = 90 + T + 50$ (for $8\text{ kg}$ block)
$T = 20 + 50$ (for $6\text{ kg}$ block)

Therefore, $F = 210\text{ N}$.

subject: Physics
text: A uniform solid cylinder of length $L$ and radius $R$ has moment of inertia about its axis equal to $I_1$. A small co-centric cylinder of length $L/2$ and radius $R/3$ carved from this cylinder has moment of inertia about its axis equals to $I_2$. The ratio $I_1 / I_2$ is ______.
solution:
Original mass $(M)$.
The removed mass $(m)$:
$$m = \rho \times \pi \left(\frac{R}{3}\right)^2 \times \frac{L}{2}$$
$$= \frac{\rho \pi R^2 L}{18} = \frac{M}{18}$$
$$I' = \frac{1}{2} \frac{M}{18} \frac{R^2}{9} = \frac{1}{324} MR^2$$
$$\frac{I}{I'} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}MR^2}{\frac{1}{324}MR^2} = 162$$

subject: Physics
text: A convex lens of refractive index $1.5$ and focal length $f = 18\text{ cm}$ is immersed in water. The difference in focal lengths of the given lens when it is in water and in air is $\alpha \times f$. The value of $\alpha$ is ________.\n(refractive index of water = $4/3$)
solution:
$ rac{1}{f_{	ext{Air}}} = \left( rac{1.5-1}{1}ight)\left( rac{1}{R_1} +  rac{1}{R_2}ight)$
$ rac{1}{f_{	ext{water}}} = \left( rac{1.5 - 4/3}{4/3}ight)\left( rac{1}{R_1} +  rac{1}{R_2}ight)$
$\Rightarrow  rac{f_{	ext{water}}}{f_{	ext{Air}}} =  rac{0.5}{0.5/4} = 4$
$\Rightarrow f_{	ext{water}} - f_{	ext{air}} = 3f$

subject: Physics
text: A beam of light consisting of wavelengths $650\text{ nm}$ and $550\text{ nm}$ illuminates the Young's double slits with separation of $2\text{ mm}$ such that the interference fringes are formed on a screen, placed at a distance of $1.2\text{ m}$ from the slits. The least distance of a point from the central maximum, where the bright fringes due to both the wavelengths coincide, is ______ $\times 10^{-5}\text{ m}$.
solution:
$y = n \frac{\lambda D}{d}$
For coincidence: $y_1 = y_2$
$n_1 \lambda_1 \frac{D}{d} = n_2 \lambda_2 \frac{D}{d}$
$\frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \frac{550}{650} = \frac{11}{13}$
Taking $n_1 = 11$, we get:
$y = 11 \times \frac{\lambda_1 D}{d} = \frac{11 \times 650 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.2}{2 \times 10^{-3}}$
$y = 429 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}$.

subject: Physics
text: A uniform wire of length $l$ of weight $w$ is suspended from the roof with a weight of $W$ at the other end. The stress in the wire at $\frac{l}{3}$ distance from the top is $\left(\frac{W}{A} + \frac{2w}{\gamma A}\right)$, where, $A$ is the cross sectional area of the wire. The value of $\gamma$ is _____.
solution:
$\sigma = \frac{T}{A} = \frac{W + \frac{w}{3}}{A}$

$$\Rightarrow \sigma = \frac{W}{A} + \frac{2w}{6A}$$

$$\therefore \gamma = 6$$

subject: Physics
text: If sunlight is focused on a paper using convex lens, it starts burning the paper in shortest time when the lens is kept at $30\text{ cm}$ above the paper. If the radius of curvature of the lens is $60\text{ cm}$ then the refractive index of the lens material is $\frac{\alpha}{10}$. The value of $\alpha$ is ___.
solution:
To burn in minimum time distance of paper must be at focus.
So $f = 30\text{ cm}$
$\frac{1}{30} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{60} - \frac{1}{-60}\right)$
$\frac{1}{30} = \frac{\mu - 1}{30}$
$\mu = 2$
$\alpha = 20$

subject: Physics
text: A body of mass $2\text{ kg}$ begins to move under the influence of time dependent force $\vec{F} = (2t\hat{i} + 6t^2\hat{j})\text{ N}$, where $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ are unit vectors along x and y-axis respectively. The power produced by the force at $t = 2\text{ s}$ is ______ $\text{W}$.
solution:
$$\vec{a} = \frac{\vec{F}}{m} = t\hat{i} + 3t^2\hat{j}$$
$$\vec{v} = \int_{0}^{2} \vec{a} \cdot \text{d}t = \left[\frac{t^2}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{3t^3}{3}\hat{j}\right]_{0}^{2}$$
$$= (2\hat{i} + 8\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$$
$$\vec{F}_{t=2} = (4\hat{i} + 24\hat{j})\text{ N}$$
$$P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = 8 + 192 = 200\text{ W}$$

subject: Physics
text:
A circular coil of radius $2\text{ cm}$ and $125$ turns carries a current of $1\text{ A}$. The coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $0.4\text{ T}$. The axis of the coil makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the direction of the magnetic field. The torque acting on the coil is $\alpha \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
$(\pi = 3.14)$
solution: $\tau = |\vec{M} \times \vec{B}| = |NI\vec{A} \times \vec{B}|$ $\tau = 125 \times 1 \times \pi \left(\frac{2}{100}\right)^2 \times 0.4 \times \sin 30^\circ = 100\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. So $\alpha = 100\pi = 314$

subject: Physics
text: The charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field of $(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})\text{ T}$ has an acceleration $\left(4\hat{i} - \frac{x}{2}\hat{j}\right)\text{ m/s}^2$. The value of $x$ is
solution:
$$\vec{F}_B \propto (\vec{V} \times \vec{B}) \Rightarrow \vec{F}_B \perp \vec{B}$$
$$\vec{a} \perp \vec{B} \Rightarrow \vec{a} \cdot \vec{B} = 0$$
$$12 - x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 12$$

subject: Physics
text: When an external resistance of $5\,\Omega$ is connected across terminals of a cell, a current of $0.25\text{ A}$ flows through it. When the $5\,\Omega$ resistor is replaced by a $2\,\Omega$ resistor, a current of $0.5\text{ A}$ flows through it. The internal resistance of the cell is ___ $\Omega$.
solution:
We know that current $i$ is given by $i = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r}$.
For $R = 5\,\Omega$, $0.25 = \frac{\varepsilon}{5 + r}$.
For $R = 2\,\Omega$, $0.5 = \frac{\varepsilon}{2 + r}$.
Dividing both equations or solving simultaneously gives $r = 1\,\Omega$.

subject: Physics
text: A three coulomb charge moves from the point $(0, -2, -5)$ to the point $(5, 1, 2)$ in an electric field expressed as $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i} + 3y^2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\text{ N/C}$. The work done in moving the charge is _______ $\text{J}$.
solution:
$\Delta U = -w_{\text{electrostatic}}$
$w_{\text{electrostatic}} = -q\Delta V$
$\Delta V = -\int 2x\mathrm{d}x - \int 3y^2\mathrm{d}y - \int 4\mathrm{d}z$
$= \left(-x^2 - y^3 - 4z\right)_{(0, -2, -5)}^{(5, 1, 2)}$
$= -62$
$w_{\text{electrostatic}} = 3(62) = 186\text{ J}$

subject: Physics
text: Two cells of emfs $1\text{ V}$ and $2\text{ V}$ and internal resistance $2\ \Omega$ and $1\ \Omega$, respectively connected in parallel, gave current of $1\text{ A}$ through an external resistance. If the polarity of one cell is reversed, then value of current through the external resistance will be $\frac{\alpha}{5}\text{ A}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _____.
solution:
For parallel combination of two cells:
$E_{eq} = \frac{\frac{E_1}{r_1} + \frac{E_2}{r_2}}{\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{2}{1}}{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{1}} = \frac{\frac{5}{2}}{\frac{3}{2}} = \frac{5}{3}\text{ V}$
$r_{eq} = \frac{r_1 r_2}{r_1 + r_2} = \frac{2 \times 1}{2 + 1} = \frac{2}{3}\text{ (Wait, let's look at the image formula: } r_{eq} = \frac{3}{2} \text{ is written, let's follow the image solution)}$
From image:
$r_{eq} = \frac{3}{2}$
$i = \frac{E_{eq}}{r_{eq} + R} \implies 1 = \frac{5/3}{3/2 + R}$
$\frac{5}{3} = \frac{3}{2} + R \implies R = \frac{5}{3} - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{1}{6}\ \Omega$
When polarity of one cell is reversed:
$E_{eq}' = \frac{\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{1}}{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{1}} = \frac{-3/2}{3/2} = -1\text{ (Magnitude } 1\text{ V)}$
$i' = \frac{E_{eq}'}{r_{eq} + R} = \frac{1}{\frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{6}} = \frac{1}{\frac{10}{6}} = \frac{6}{10} = \frac{3}{5}\text{ A}$
Given current is $\frac{\alpha}{5}\text{ A}$, so $\frac{\alpha}{5} = \frac{3}{5} \implies \alpha = 3$.

subject: Physics
text: The stored charge in the capacitor in steady state of the following circuit is _______ $\mu\text{C}$.\n(Circuit diagram showing resistors $5\,\Omega$, $12\,\Omega$, $4\,\Omega$, $10\,\Omega$, $4\,\Omega$, $2\,\Omega$, $2\,\Omega$ and a $100\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor with $12\text{V}$ source).
solution:
At steady state,
$I = \frac{E}{R_{eq}} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\text{A}$
$I_1 = I_2 = 1\text{A}$
$I_3 = I_4 = \frac{1}{2}\text{A}$
$V_{AB} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 = 2\text{V}$
Charge on capacitor
$Q = CV_{AB} = 100 \times 2 = 200\text{ }\mu\text{C}$

subject: Physics
text: In a microscope the objective is having focal length $f_0 = 2 \text{ cm}$ and eye-piece is having focal length $f_e = 4 \text{ cm}$. The tube length is $32 \text{ cm}$. The magnification produced by this microscope for normal adjustment is $\qquad$.
solution:
$m \approx \frac{lD}{f_0f_e}$
$= \frac{32}{2} \times \frac{25}{4}$
$m = 100$

subject: Physics
text: A diatomic gas ($\gamma = 1.4$) does $100\text{ J}$ of work when it is expanded isobarically. Then the heat given to the gas _______ $\text{J}$.
solution:
$w = 100\text{ J} = nR\Delta T$ for isobaric process.
$Q = nC_p\Delta T = \left(\frac{f}{2} + 1\right) nR\Delta T$
$= \frac{7}{2} \cdot (100) = 350\text{ Joule}.

subject: Physics
text: Inductance of a coil with $10^4$ turns is $10\text{ mH}$ and it is connected to a dc source of $10\text{ V}$ with internal resistance of $10\Omega$. The energy density in the inductor when the current reaches $\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)$ of its maximum value is $\alpha\pi \times \frac{1}{e^2}\text{ J/m}^3$. The value of $\alpha$ is ___ . ($\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ Tm/A}$).
solution:
$L = 10 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}$
$N = 10^4$
$I_0 = \frac{10}{10} = 1\text{ A}$ (max current)
$I = \frac{1}{e}$
$E_d = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$
$B = \mu_0 n I$
$L = \mu_0 n^2 \pi R^2 \ell$
$E_d = \frac{\mu_0 n^2 I^2}{2}$
$= \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10^8 \times \frac{1}{e^2}}{2}$
$= \frac{20\pi}{e^2}$
Therefore, $\alpha = 20$.

subject: Physics
text: An insulated cylinder of volume $60\text{ cm}^3$ is filled with a gas at $27^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $2\text{ atmospheric pressure}$. Then the gas is compressed making the final volume as $20\text{ cm}^3$ while allowing the temperature to rise to $77^{\circ}\text{C}$. The final pressure is ______ atmospheric pressure.
solution:
Using ideal gas equation $PV = nRT$:
$\frac{P_1 V_1}{R T_1} = \frac{P_2 V_2}{R T_2}$
$\frac{2 \times 10^5 \times 60}{300} = \frac{P_2 \times 20}{350}$
$P_2 = \frac{2 \times 10^5 \times 7 \times 3}{6}$
$P_2 = 7 \times 10^5 = 7\text{ atm}$

subject: Physics
text: The space between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor of capacitance $C$ (without any dielectric) is now filled with three dielectric slabs of dielectric constants $K_1 = 2$, $K_2 = 3$, and $K_3 = 5$ (as shown in the figure). If new capacitance is $\frac{n}{3}C$ then the value of n is $\rule{2cm}{0.15mm}$.
solution:
$C_1 = \frac{5 \epsilon_0 A / 2}{d / 2} = \frac{5 \epsilon_0 A}{d} = 5C$
$C_2 = \frac{2 \epsilon_0 A / 2}{d / 2} = \frac{2 \epsilon_0 A}{d} = 2C$
$C_1 \text{ & } C_2 \text{ in series: } C' = \frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2} = \frac{(5C)(2C)}{7C} = \frac{10}{7}C$
$C_3 = \frac{3 \epsilon_0 A / 2}{d / 2} = 3C$
$C_4 = \frac{2 \epsilon_0 A / 2}{d / 2} = 2C$
$C_4 \text{ & } C_3 \text{ in series: } C'' = \frac{(2C)(3C)}{5C} = \frac{6}{5}C$
$C' \text{ & } C'' \text{ in parallel: } C_{eq} = C \left(\frac{6}{5} + \frac{10}{7}\right) = C \left(\frac{42 + 50}{35}\right) = \left(\frac{92}{35}\right)C$
$$\frac{92}{35}C = \frac{nC}{3}$$
$$n = \frac{92 \times 3}{35} = 7.9 \implies n \approx 8$$

subject: Physics
text: The velocity of sound in air is doubled when the temperature is raised from $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $\alpha^{\circ}\text{C}$. The value of $\alpha$ is ______.
solution:
We know that the velocity of sound in gas is given by:
$$V = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}$$
Therefore, $V \propto \sqrt{T}$, so:
$$\frac{V_1}{V_2} = \sqrt{\frac{T_1}{T_2}}$$
Given that $V_1 = V_0$, $T_1 = 0^{\circ}\text{C} = 273\text{ K}$, and $V_2 = 2V_0$:
$$\frac{V_0}{2V_0} = \sqrt{\frac{273}{T_2}}$$
$$\frac{1}{4} = \frac{273}{T_2}$$
$$T_2 = 4 \times 273 = \alpha + 273$$
$$\alpha = 3 \times 273 = 819^{\circ}\text{C}$$

subject: Physics
text: Sixty four rain drops of radius $1\text{ mm}$ each falling down with a terminal velocity of $10\text{ cm/s}$ coalesce to form a bigger drop. The terminal velocity of bigger drop is ______ $\text{cm/s}$.
solution:
Terminal velocity $V_T = \frac{2r^2g}{9\eta}[-\rho]
$V_T \propto r^2$

Volume conservation for 64 drops:
$64 \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi R_1^3\right) = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_2^3$
$R_2 = 4R_1$

$\frac{(V_T)_1}{(V_T)_2} = \left(\frac{R_1}{R_2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2$

$\frac{10}{(V_T)_2} = \frac{1}{16}$

$(V_T)_2 = 160\text{ cm/sec}$

subject: Physics
text:
A soap bubble of surface tension $0.04\text{ N/m}$ is blown to a diameter of $7\text{ cm}$. If $(15000 - x)\ \mu\text{J}$ of work is done in blowing it further to make its diameter $14\text{ cm}$, then the value of x is ______.
($\pi = 22/7$)

subject: Physics
text: The equivalent resistance between the points $A$ and $B$ in the following circuit is $\frac{x}{5}\ \Omega$. The value of $x$ is ________.
solution:
Applying Kirchhoff's laws to the bridge circuit:
$6i_1 + 3(2i_1 - i) = 3(i - i_1)$
$\Rightarrow 15i_1 = 6i \Rightarrow i_1 =  rac{2}{5}i \quad 	ext{--- (1)}$
$3(i - i_1) + 6i_1 = 1$
$3i + 3i_1 = 1$
$\left(3 +  rac{6}{5}ight)i = 1$
$\Rightarrow i =  rac{5}{21}	ext{A} =  rac{1	ext{V}}{R_{	ext{eq}}} \Rightarrow R_{	ext{eq}} =  rac{21}{5}\ \Omega$

subject: Physics
text: A fly wheel having mass $3\text{ kg}$ and radius $5\text{ m}$ is free to rotate about a horizontal axis. A string having negligible mass is wound around the wheel and the loose end of the string is connected to a $3\text{ kg}$ mass. The mass is kept at rest initially and released. Kinetic energy of the wheel when the mass descends by $3\text{ m}$ is ______ $\text{J}$. ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
solution:
By conservation of energy:
$mg h = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \quad \text{--- (i)}$
and $v = \omega R \quad \text{--- (ii)}$
Substituting $I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2$ where $M = 3\text{ kg}$, $m = 3\text{ kg}$, $h = 3\text{ m}$, $R = 5\text{ m}$:
$mg \times 3 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{M R^2}{2}\right) \omega^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v^2$
Since $\omega R = v$, $\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{M R^2}{2}\right) \frac{v^2}{R^2} = \frac{1}{4} M v^2$
$3 \times 10 \times 3 = \left(\frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{2}\right) v^2 \text{ (wait, using mass terms carefully)}$
From solution steps in image:
$g \times 3 = \frac{3}{4} v^2$
K.E. of flywheel = $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{m R^2}{2} \times \omega^2 = \frac{1}{4} m v^2$
$= \frac{1}{4} \times 3 \times 40 = 30\text{ Joule}$.

subject: Physics
text:
A tube is filled with water and a wooden cube $10\,\text{cm} \times 10\,\text{cm} \times 10\,\text{cm}$ is placed in the water. The wooden cube is found to float on the water with a part of it submerged in water. When a metal coin is placed on the wooden cube, the submerged part is increased by $3.87\,\text{cm}$. The mass of the metal coin is _____ gram.
(Take water density as $1\,\text{g/cm}^3$ and density of wood as $0.4\,\text{g/cm}^3$)
solution:
Weight of coin = Additional upthrust

$$\Rightarrow m_c g = \rho_{\ell} V_{\text{add}} g$$

$$\Rightarrow m_c = 1 \times 3.87 \times (10)^2$$

$$\Rightarrow m_c = 387\,\text{gram}$$

subject: Physics
text: Moment of inertia about an axis AB for a rod of mass $40\text{ kg}$ and length $3\text{ m}$ is same as that of a solid sphere of mass $10\text{ kg}$ and radius R about an axis parallel to AB axis with separation of $3\text{ m}$ as shown in figure below. The value of R is given as $\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2}}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _____.
solution:
$I_{\text{Rod}} = I_{\text{SS}}$
$\frac{M_1 L^2}{3} = \left(\frac{2}{5} m_2 R^2 + m_2 L^2\right)$
$\frac{40 \times (3)^2}{3} = \frac{2}{5} \times 10 \times R^2 + 10 \times (3)^2$
$120 = 4R^2 + 90$
$4R^2 = 30$
$R = \sqrt{\frac{15}{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2}}$
$\alpha = 15$

subject: Physics
text: An inductor of $10\text{ mH}$, capacitor of $0.1\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ and a resistor of $100\text{ }\Omega$ are connected in series across an a.c power supply $220\text{ V}$, $70\text{ Hz}$. The power factor of the given circuit is $0.5$. The difference in the inductive reactance and capacitance reactance is $\sqrt{3}\alpha\text{ }\Omega$. The value of $\alpha$ is ______.
solution:
$$\cos\phi = 0.5 = \frac{1}{2}$$
$$\phi = 60^{\circ}$$
$$\tan\phi = \frac{|x_L - x_C|}{R}$$
$$\tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3} = \frac{x_L - x_C}{R}$$
$$|x_L - x_C| = R\sqrt{3} = 100\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{3}\alpha$$
$$\alpha = 100$$

subject: Physics
text: In a double slit experiment, when one of the slits is covered by a transparent mica sheet of refractive index $1.56$, the central fringe shifts to the position of $7^{\text{th}}$ bright fringe, obtained with both slits uncovered. If the light source wavelength is $450\text{ nm}$, the thickness of mica sheet is $\alpha \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______.
solution: $\Delta y = (\mu - 1)t \frac{D}{d} = 7 \frac{\lambda D}{d}$ $\Rightarrow (\mu - 1)t = 7\lambda$ $\Rightarrow (1.56 - 1)t = 7 \times 450\text{ nm}$ $\Rightarrow t = 5625\text{ nm}$

subject: Physics
text: In the given circuit below inductance values of $L_1, L_2$ and $L_3$ are same. The magnetic energy stored in the entire circuit is $(U_t)$ and that stored in the $L_2$ inductor is $(U_{\ell})$. $(U_t / U_{\ell})$ is _______. (Ignore the mutual inductance if any)
solution:
Magnetic energy of inductor is $U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$
So $U_t = \frac{1}{2}LI^2 + \frac{1}{2}L\left(\frac{I}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{1}{2}L\left(\frac{I}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{3}{4}LI^2$
$$U_{\ell} = \frac{1}{2}L\left(\frac{I}{2}\right)^2 \Rightarrow \frac{U_t}{U_{\ell}} = 6$$

subject: Physics
text: A circular loop of radius $20\text{ cm}$ and resistance $2\,\Omega$ is placed in a time varying magnetic field $\vec{B} = (2t^2 + 2t + 3)\,\text{T}$. At $t = 0$, for the plane of the loop being perpendicular to the magnetic field and, the induced current in the loop at $t = 3\text{ s}$ is $\frac{\alpha}{50}\text{ A}$. The value of $\alpha$ is ___ (Take $\pi = 22/7$)
solution:
Magnetic flux $\phi = B \cdot \pi r^2$.
Induced emf $\varepsilon = \frac{d\phi}{dt} = \pi r^2 \frac{dB}{dt}$.
Induced current $i = \frac{\varepsilon}{R} = \frac{\pi r^2}{R}\left(\frac{dB}{dt}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^2 (4t + 2)$.
For $t = 3$, $i = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{1}{25} \times 14 = \frac{44}{50}$.
Therefore, $\alpha = 44$.

subject: Physics
text: A certain gas is isothermally compressed to $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\text{rd}}$ of its initial volume ($V_0 = 3\text{ litre}$) by applying required pressure. If the bulk modulus of the gas is $3 \times 10^5\text{ N/m}^2$, the magnitude of work done on the gas is _______ $\text{J}$.
solution:
For isothermal process initially $B = P_0$.
$W = nRT \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$
$= P_0 V_0 \ln\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)$
$W = BV_0 \ln\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)$
$W = -988.75\text{ J} \approx 989\text{ J}$
Note: Bulk modulus of gas for isothermal process is not constant. In the given solution we have considered it as initial bulk modulus.

subject: Physics
text: A concave mirror of focal length $10\text{ cm}$ from an image which is double the size of object when the object is placed at two different positions. The distance between the two positions of the object is _____ $\text{cm}$.
solution:
Case I: $v = 2u$ (Real image, magnification $m = -2$)
$$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$
$$\frac{1}{-2u} + \frac{1}{-u} = \frac{1}{-f}$$
$$\frac{3}{2u} = \frac{1}{f} \implies u_1 = \frac{3f}{2}$$
Case II: $v = -2u$ (Virtual image, magnification $m = +2$)
$$\frac{1}{+2u} + \frac{1}{-u} = \frac{1}{-f}$$
$$\frac{-1}{2u} = \frac{1}{-f} \implies u_2 = \frac{f}{2}$$
Distance between the two positions of the object:
$$\Delta u = u_1 - u_2 = \frac{3f}{2} - \frac{f}{2} = f = 10\text{ cm}$$

subject: Physics
text: Two masses of $3.4\text{ kg}$ and $2.5\text{ kg}$ are accelerated from an initial speed of $5\text{ m/s}$ and $12\text{ m/s}$, respectively. The distances traversed by the masses in the $5^{\text{th}}$ second are $104\text{ m}$ and $129\text{ m}$, respectively. The ratio of their momenta after $10\text{ s}$ is $\frac{x}{8}$. The value of $x$ is _______.
solution:
$S = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1) \Rightarrow 104 = 5 + \frac{a}{2}(9) \Rightarrow a = 22\text{ m/s}^2$
$129 = 12 + \frac{a}{2} \times 9 \Rightarrow a = 26\text{ m/s}^2$
$\frac{p_1}{p_2} = \frac{(5 + 22 \times 10)3.4}{(12 + 26 \times 10)(2.5)} = \frac{225 \times (3.4)}{272 \times 2.5} = \frac{9}{8}$

subject: Physics
text: A cup of water at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ (system) is placed in a microwave oven and the oven is turned on for one minute during which, the water begins to boil. Which of the following option is true?
solution:

subject: Physics
text: The work functions of two metals ($	ext{M}_A$ and $	ext{M}_B$) are in the $1 : 2$ ratio. When these metals are exposed to photons of energy $6\text{ eV}$, the kinetic energy of liberated electrons of $	ext{M}_A : 	ext{M}_B$ is in the ratio of $2.642 : 1$. The work functions (in $	ext{eV}$) of $	ext{M}_A$ and $	ext{M}_B$ are respectively.
solution:
Einstein's photoelectric equation is given by $\text{KE}_{\text{max}} = E - \phi$.
For metal A: $(\text{KE}_{\text{max}})_1 = 6 - \phi_1 \quad \dots\dots \text{(1)}$
For metal B: $(\text{KE}_{\text{max}})_2 = 6 - \phi_2 \quad \dots\dots \text{(2)}$
Given $\phi_2 = 2\phi_1$ and $\frac{(\text{KE}_{\text{max}})_1}{(\text{KE}_{\text{max}})_2} = \frac{2.642}{1}$.
Dividing eq. (1) by eq. (2):
$$\frac{2.642}{1} = \frac{6 - \phi_1}{6 - 2\phi_1}$$
Solving for $\phi_1$:
$$\phi_1 = 2.3\text{ eV}$$
$$\phi_2 = 4.6\text{ eV}$$

subject: Physics
text:
Regarding self-inductance :

 A : The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry.

 B : Self-inductance does not depend on the permeability of the medium.

 C : Self-induced e.m.f. opposes any change in the current in a circuit.

 D : Self-inductance is electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.

 E : Work needs to be done against self-induced e.m.f. in establishing the current.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Self inductance of coil:
$$L = \frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{2\pi R}$$
- It depends on geometry (A is correct).
- It depends on the permeability of the medium (B is incorrect).
- Self-induced e.m.f. opposes any change in the current (C is correct).
- Self-inductance is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics (D is correct).
- Work needs to be done against self-induced e.m.f. (E is correct).
Therefore, A, C, D, E only are correct.

text: A ball having kinetic energy $\text{KE}$, is projected at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ from the horizontal. What will be the kinetic energy of ball at the highest point of its flight?
solution:
Initial K.E,
$$\text{K.E.} = \frac{1}{2} mu^2$$
Speed at highest point
$$V = u \cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{u}{2}$$
$$\therefore \text{KE}_2 = \frac{1}{2} m \left(\frac{u}{2}\right)^2$$
$$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} mu^2$$
$$= \frac{\text{KE}}{4}$$

text: Consider a parallel plate capacitor of area A (of each plate) and separation 'd' between the plates. If E is the electric field and $\varepsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space between the plates, then potential energy stored in the capacitor is :-
solution: Energy density $u = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 \text{E}^2$. Total potential energy $U = u \times \text{Volume} = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 \text{E}^2 \times (Ad)$. Hence, correct option is (1).

text: Two capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected in parallel to a battery. Charge-time graph is shown below for the two capacitors. The energy stored with them are $U_1$ and $U_2$, respectively. Which of the given statements is true?
solution:
Potential difference, $V$ is same for both capacitors in parallel.
Energy stored is given by $U =  rac{1}{2}CV^2$.
From the given charge-time graph, at any time $t$, charge $q_1 < q_2$.
Since $q = CV$ and $V$ is constant, $q \propto C$, which implies $C_1 < C_2$ or $C_2 > C_1$.
Since $U \propto C$, we get $U_1 < U_2$, or $U_2 > U_1$.

text: A light wave is propagating with plane wave fronts of the type $x + y + z = \text{constant}$. The angle made by the direction of wave propagation with the x-axis is :
solution:
The direction of propagation of light is perpendicular to the wave front and is symmetric about x, y and z axis.
$\therefore$ Angle made by the light with x, y & z axis is same.
$\therefore \cos\alpha = \cos\beta = \cos\gamma$ ($\alpha$, $\beta$ & $\gamma$ are angle made by light with x, y & z axis respectively)
Also $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$ [Sum of direction cosines]
$\therefore \alpha = \cos^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

Reason (R) : In absence of an external electric field, the different permanent dipoles of a polar dielectric substance are oriented in random directions.

R : If $\vec{E}$ is absent, polar dielectric remain polar & are randomly oriented.
Thus, (A) is not correct but (R) is correct.

subject: Physics
text: During the melting of a slab of ice at $273\text{ K}$ at atmospheric pressure :

options.1: Internal energy of ice-water system remains unchanged.
options.2: Positive work is done by the ice-water system on the atmosphere.
options.3: Internal energy of the ice-water system decreases.
options.4: Positive work is done on the ice-water system by the atmosphere.

solution: Volume decreases during melting of ice so positive work is done on ice water system by atmosphere. Heat absorbed by ice water so $\Delta Q$ is positive, work done by ice water system is negative. Hence by first law of thermodynamics $\Delta U = \Delta Q + \Delta W = \text{Positive}$. So internal energy increases.

$MB = 160$

subject: Physics
text: A radioactive material $P$ first decays into $Q$ and then $Q$ decays to non-radioactive material $R$. Which of the following figure represents time dependent mass of $P$, $Q$ and $R$?

options.1: Graph with decreasing P, and increasing Q and R curves starting from origin.
options.2: Graph with decreasing P, initially increasing then decreasing Q, and increasing R curve starting from origin.
options.3: Graph with increasing P, decreasing Q and R.
options.4: Graph with P increasing, R and Q decreasing.

solution:
For radioactive decay series $P \rightarrow Q \rightarrow R$:
- The mass of $P$ decreases exponentially with time.
- The mass of $Q$ initially increases as it is formed from $P$, reaches a maximum, and then decreases as it decays into $R$.
- The mass of $R$ (non-radioactive end product) increases continuously with time and eventually saturates.
Therefore, option (2) represents the correct time-dependent masses.

subject: Physics
text: Two harmonic waves moving in the same direction superimpose to form a wave $x = a \cos(1.5t) \cos(50.5t)$ where $t$ is in seconds. Find the period with which they beat (close to nearest integer)
solution:
The given equation can be written as
$x = \frac{a}{2} \cos[1.5 + 50.5]t + \frac{a}{2} \cos[50.5 - 1.5]t$
$x = \frac{a}{2} \cos[52t] + \frac{a}{2} \cos[49t]$
Here, $2\pi f_1 = 52$ & $2\pi f_2 = 49$
$f_1 = \frac{52}{2\pi}$, $f_2 = \frac{49}{2\pi}$
$\therefore f_{\text{Beat}} = f_1 - f_2 = \frac{3}{2\pi} \text{ Hz}$
$\therefore T_{\text{Beat}} = \frac{1}{f_{\text{Beat}}} = \frac{2\pi}{3} \text{ sec} = 2.09 \text{ sec} \approx 2 \text{ sec}$

text: A small rigid spherical ball of mass M is dropped in a long vertical tube containing glycerine. The velocity of the ball becomes constant after some time. If the density of glycerine is half of the density of the ball, then the viscous force acting on the ball will be (consider g as acceleration due to gravity)
solution: When velocity becomes constant, acceleration $a = 0$. Forces acting on the ball are downward gravitational force $mg$, upward buoyant force $F_B$, and upward viscous force $f$. \n$mg - F_B - f = 0 \implies mg - \frac{mg}{2} - f = 0 \implies f = \frac{mg}{2}$.

text: A light hollow cube of side length $10\text{ cm}$ and mass $10\text{ g}$, is floating in water. It is pushed down and released to execute simple harmonic oscillations. text: Two charges $7\text{ }\mu\text{c}$ and $-4\text{ }\mu\text{c}$ are placed at $(-7\text{ cm}, 0, 0)$ and $(7\text{ cm}, 0, 0)$ respectively. Given, $\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{ N}^{-1}\text{ m}^{-2}$, the electrostatic potential energy of the charge configuration is :
solution:
P.E. of two charges
$$u = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r}$$
$$r = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$|
$$= 14\text{ cm}$$
$$\therefore u = \frac{9\times 10^9 \times 7\times 10^{-6} \times (-4)\times 10^{-6}}{14\times 10^{-2}}$$
$$= -1.8\text{ J}$$

subject: Physics
text: What is the relative decrease in focal length of a lens for an increase in optical power by $0.1\text{ D}$ from $2.5\text{ D}$? ['D' stands for dioptre]
solution: When $P = 2.5\text{ D}$, $F = \frac{1}{P} = \frac{1}{2.5}$. When $P' = 2.6\text{ D}$, $F' = \frac{1}{P'} = \frac{1}{2.6}$. Relative decrease in focal length = $\frac{F - F'}{F} = \frac{\frac{2}{5} - \frac{5}{13}}{\frac{2}{5}} = 1 - \frac{25}{26} = \frac{1}{26} = 0.04$. Hence, option (1).

(B) Ultraviolet rays ($\lambda_2$)
(C) Infrared rays ($\lambda_3$)
(D) X-rays ($\lambda_4$)
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :-
solution:

$$\text{X-rays} \to \text{U.V rays} \to \text{Visible} \to \text{IR} \to \text{Micro waves} \to \text{Radio waves}$$
Therefore, $\lambda_4 < \lambda_2 < \lambda_3 < \lambda_1$.

subject: Physics
text:
In the experiment for measurement of viscosity '$\eta$' of given liquid with a ball having radius $R$, consider following statements:
A. Graph between terminal velocity $V$ and $R$ will be a parabola.
B. The terminal velocities of different diameter balls are constant for a given liquid.
C. Measurement of terminal velocity is dependent on the temperature.
D. This experiment can be utilized to assess the density of a given liquid.
E. If balls are dropped with some initial speed, the value of $\eta$ will change.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Terminal velocity is given by $V_T = rac{2}{9} R^2 rac{g}{\eta} (d - \rho)$.
A. $V_T \propto R^2$, so the graph between $V$ and $R$ is a parabola. (True)
B. Terminal velocity depends on diameter ($R$), so it is not constant for different diameters. (False)
C. Viscosity $\eta$ depends strongly on temperature, hence terminal velocity measurement is temperature dependent. (True)
D. Since $\rho$ (density of liquid) appears in the formula, this experiment can be used to find $\rho$. (True)
E. Terminal velocity is independent of the initial speed of the ball. (False)
Hence, statements A, C, and D are correct.

$U = 1.77 \times 10^3\text{ J/m}^3$

subject: Physics
text: Two projectiles are fired with same initial speed from same point on ground at angles of $(45^\circ - \alpha)$ and $(45^\circ + \alpha)$, respectively, with the horizontal direction. The ratio of their maximum heights attained is :
solution:
$$H_{\text{Max}} = \frac{(u\sin\theta)^2}{2g}$$
$$\frac{(H_{\text{max}})_1}{(H_{\text{max}})_2} = \frac{u^2 \sin^2(45-\alpha)}{u^2 \sin^2(45+\alpha)}$$
$$= \frac{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\alpha - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\alpha\right)^2}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\alpha + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\alpha\right)^2}$$
$$= \frac{1 - \sin 2\alpha}{1 + \sin 2\alpha}$$

text: The equation for real gas is given by $\left(P + \frac{a}{V^2}\right)(V - b) = RT$, where P, V, T and R are the pressure, volume, temperature and gas constant, respectively. The dimension of $ab^{-2}$ is equivalent to that of :
solution:
$\left(P + \frac{a}{V^2}\right)(V - b) = RT$
$\therefore [a] = [P]\left[V^2\right] = \text{ML}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}\text{L}^6 = \text{ML}^5\text{T}^{-2}$
$[b] = [V] = \text{L}^3$
$[ab^{-2}] = \text{ML}^5\text{T}^{-2}\text{L}^{-6} = \text{ML}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}$
Dimension of energy density.

subject: Physics
text:
In a moving coil galvanometer, two moving coils $M_1$ and $M_2$ have the following particulars :
$R_1 = 5\;\Omega$, $N_1 = 15$, $A_1 = 3.6 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{m}^2$, $B_1 = 0.25\;\text{T}$
$R_2 = 7\;\Omega$, $N_2 = 21$, $A_2 = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{m}^2$, $B_2 = 0.50\;\text{T}$
Assuming that torsional constant of the springs are same for both coils, what will be the ratio of voltage sensitivity of $M_1$ and $M_2$ ?
solution:
Voltage sensitivity $= \frac{\theta}{V} = \frac{NAB}{cR}$
Ratio $= \left(\frac{N_1 A_1 B_1}{N_2 A_2 B_2}\right) \frac{R_2}{R_1} = \frac{15 \times 3.6 \times 0.25}{21 \times 1.8 \times 0.5} \times \frac{7}{5} = \frac{1}{1}$

subject: Physics
text: Consider a completely full cylindrical water tank of height $1.6\text{ m}$ and cross-sectional area $0.5\text{ m}^2$. It has a small hole in its side at a height $90\text{ cm}$ from the bottom. Assume, the cross-sectional area of the hole to be negligibly small as compared to that of the water tank. If a load $50\text{ kg}$ is applied at the top surface of the water in the tank then the velocity of the water coming out at the instant when the hole is opened is : ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
solution:
Apply Bernoulli equation between points 1 & 2:
$$P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho gh = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + 0$$
$$P_0 + \frac{mg}{A} + \rho g \frac{70}{100} = P_0 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2$$
$$\frac{5000}{0.5} + 10^3 \times 10 \times \frac{70}{100} = \frac{1}{2} \times 10^3 v_2^2$$
$$10^3 + 10^3 \times 7 = \frac{10^3}{2} v_2^2$$
$$v_2^2 = 16$$
$$v_2 = 4\text{ m/s}$$
As the tank area is large $v_1$ is negligible compared to $v_2$.

subject: Physics
text: In the resonance experiment, two air columns (closed at one end) of $100\text{ cm}$ and $120\text{ cm}$ long, give $15$ beats per second when each one is sounding in the respective fundamental modes. The velocity of sound in the air column is :
solution:
Fundamental frequency in close/organ pipe
$f = \frac{v}{4\ell}$
$f_1 = \frac{v}{4\ell_1}$ & $f_2 = \frac{v}{4\ell_2}$
$\text{Beat} = (f_1 - f_2) = \frac{v}{4}\left(\frac{1}{\ell_1} - \frac{1}{\ell_2}\right)$
$15 = \frac{v}{4}\left(\frac{1}{1} - \frac{1}{1.2}\right)$
$v = \left(\frac{15 \times 4 \times 1.2}{0.2}\right) = 60 \times 6 = 360\text{ m/s}$
subtopic: Waves, Resonance, Organ Pipes & Doppler Effect

subject: Physics
text: A small mirror of mass $m$ is suspended by a massless thread of length $l$. Then the small angle through which the thread will be deflected when a short pulse of laser of energy $E$ falls normal on the mirror ($c$ = speed of light in vacuum and $g$ = acceleration due to gravity)
solution: Force due to beam assuming complete reflection: $F = \frac{2P}{C} = \frac{2}{C}\frac{dE}{dt}$; $P$ is power. Change in momentum of mirror: $m(V - 0) = \int Fdt = \frac{2}{C} \int dE = \frac{2E}{C}$. Now using work energy theorem: $W_g = \Delta k \implies -mg\ell(1-\cos\theta) = 0 - \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies g\ell\left(2\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}\right) = \frac{v^2}{2}$. As $\theta$ is small, $g\ell 2 \left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\frac{4E^2}{m^2c^2} \implies g\ell \theta^2 = \frac{4E^2}{m^2c^2} \implies \theta = \frac{2E}{mc\sqrt{g\ell}}$

subject: Physics
text: There are '$n$' number of identical electric bulbs, each is designed to draw a power $p$ independently from the mains supply. They are now joined in series across the main supply. The total power drawn by the combination is :
solution:
Resistance of each bulb $R = \frac{V^2}{p}$.
When $n$ identical bulbs are connected in series, the total resistance $R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \dots + R_n = nR$.
The total power $P_s$ is given by:
$$\frac{V^2}{P_s} = \frac{V^2}{P} + \frac{V^2}{P} + \dots + \frac{V^2}{P} = n \frac{V^2}{P}$$
$$P_s = \frac{P}{n}$$

text: An air bubble of radius $0.1\text{ cm}$ lies at a depth of $20\text{ cm}$ below the free surface of a liquid of density $1000\text{ kg/m}^3$. Pressure in air bubble $= P_0 + \rho gh + \frac{2T}{R}$. $P_{\text{in}} - P_0 = \rho gh + \frac{2T}{R} = 2100$. $\frac{2T}{R} = 2100 - \rho gh$. $T = \frac{R}{2}(2100 - 10^3 \times 10 \times 0.2) = \frac{1}{20}(2100 - 2000) \times 10^{-2} = 0.05$. text:
Consider following statements:
A. Surface tension arises due to extra energy of the molecules at the interior as compared to the molecules at the surface, of a liquid.
B. As the temperature of liquid rises, the coefficient of viscosity increases.
C. As the temperature of gas increases, the coefficient of viscosity increases.
D. The onset of turbulence is determined by Reynold's number.
E. In a steady flow two stream lines never intersect.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
solution:
A. Surface tension arises due to extra energy of molecules at the *surface* compared to the *interior*, not vice versa. (False)
B. As temperature of liquid rises, viscosity decreases. (False)
C. As temperature of gas increases, viscosity increases due to increased molecular momentum transfer. (True)
D. Onset of turbulence is determined by Reynolds number ($R_e$). (True)
E. In steady flow, two streamlines can never intersect because at the point of intersection, fluid particles would have two different velocities, which is impossible. (True)
Therefore, statements C, D, and E are correct.

text: Consider a rectangular sheet of solid material of length $\ell = 9\text{ cm}$ and width $d = 4\text{ cm}$. The coefficient of linear expansion is $\alpha = 3.1 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}$ at room temperature and one atmospheric pressure. The mass of sheet $m = 0.1\text{ kg}$ and the specific heat capacity $C_v = 900\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$. If the amount of heat supplied to the material is $8.1 \times 10^2\text{ J}$ then change in area of the rectangular sheet is :-
solution:
Given:
$\Delta Q = ms\Delta T$
$8.1 \times 10^2 = 0.1 \times 900 \times \Delta T$
$\Delta T = \frac{810}{90} = 9\text{ K}$ (or $\Delta Q = 810\text{ J}$, $m=0.1$, $s=900$)
Initial area $A_0 = \ell \times d = 9\text{ cm} \times 4\text{ cm} = 36\text{ cm}^2 = 36 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$.
Change in area:
$$\Delta A = A_0 \gamma \Delta T = A_0 (2\alpha) \Delta T$$
$$\Delta A = (36 \times 10^{-4}) \times 2 \times (3.1 \times 10^{-5}) \times \frac{8.1 \times 10^2}{0.1 \times 900}$$
Calculating directly:
$$\Delta A = A_0 (2\alpha) \Delta T = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$$

subject: Physics
text: Three infinitely long wires with linear charge density $\lambda$ are placed along the x-axis, y-axis and z-axis respectively. Which of the following denotes an equipotential surface?
solution:
For an infinitely long straight wire along the z-axis with linear charge density $\lambda$, the electric potential at a distance $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ is given by $V_z = -2k\lambda \ln(r) + C = -k\lambda \ln(x^2 + y^2) + C$.
Similarly, for wires along the x-axis and y-axis, the potentials are dependent on $(y^2 + z^2)$ and $(z^2 + x^2)$ respectively.
The total potential $V$ at any point $(x, y, z)$ is the sum of potentials due to all three wires:
$V = -k\lambda [\ln(x^2 + y^2) + \ln(y^2 + z^2) + \ln(z^2 + x^2)] + C'$
$V = -k\lambda \ln[(x^2 + y^2)(y^2 + z^2)(z^2 + x^2)] + C'$
For an equipotential surface, $V = \text{constant}$, which means $(x^2 + y^2)(y^2 + z^2)(z^2 + x^2) = \text{constant}$.

text: A long straight wire of a circular cross-section with radius '$a$' carries a steady current $I$. The current $I$ is a uniformly distributed across this cross-section. The plot of magnitude of magnetic field $B$ with distance $r$ from the centre of the wire is given by

options.1: Graph increasing linearly from origin up to $r=a$, then decreasing as $\frac{1}{r}$
options.2: Graph starting at $r=a$ and decreasing as $\frac{1}{r}$
options.3: Graph starting at $B_0$ and decreasing exponentially
options.4: Graph constant up to $r=a$, then decreasing as $\frac{1}{r}$

solution:
For $r \le a$ (inside the wire):
$B_{in} \propto r$

For $r > a$ (outside the wire):
$B_{out} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \implies B_{net} \propto \frac{1}{r}$

Thus, the magnetic field increases linearly with $r$ inside the wire up to $r=a$ and then decreases inversely with distance outside the wire. This corresponds to graph (1).

text: A radioactive nucleus $n_2$ has 3 times the decay constant as compared to the decay constant of another radioactive nucleus $n_1$. If initial number of both nuclei are the same, what is the ratio of number of nuclei of $n_2$ to the number of nuclei of $n_1$, after one half-life of $n_1$?
solution:
$N_2 = N_0 e^{-3\lambda_1 t}$
$N_1 = N_0 e^{-\lambda_1 t}$
$\frac{N_2}{N_1} = e^{-2\lambda_1 t}$
For half life of $n_1$, $t = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda_1}$
$\frac{N_0}{2} = N_0 e^{-\lambda_1 t} \implies \lambda_1 t = \ln 2 \implies t = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda_1}$
Substitute $t$:
$\frac{N_2}{N_1} = e^{-2\lambda_1 \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda_1}} = e^{-2\ln 2} = e^{\ln(2^{-2})} = \frac{1}{4}$

text: Consider a long thin conducting wire carrying a uniform current $I$. A particle having mass '$M$' and charge '$q$' is released at a distance '$a$' from the wire with a speed $v_0$ along the direction of current in the wire. The particle gets attracted to the wire due to magnetic force. The particle turns round when it is at distance $x$ from the wire. The value of $x$ is [$\mu_0$ is vacuum permeability]
solution: Velocity vector $\vec{V} = -v_x \hat{i} + v_y \hat{j}$. Magnetic field $\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}(-\hat{k})$. Magnetic force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}) = \frac{\mu_0 Iq}{2\pi r}[-v_x \hat{j} - v_y \hat{i}]$. Accelerations are $a_x = -\frac{\mu_0 Iq}{2\pi m}\frac{v_y}{r}$ and $a_y = \frac{\mu_0 Iq}{2\pi m}\frac{v_x}{r}$. Integrating yields the turning point distance $x = a e^{\frac{-4\pi mv_0}{q\mu_0 I}}$.

text: From the combination of resistors with resistance values $R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = 5\;\Omega$ and $R_4 = 10\;\Omega$, which of the following combination is the best circuit to get an equivalent resistance of $6\;\Omega$?
solution:
For combination (1):
Upper branch has $R_1$ and $R_2$ in series: $R_{12} = R_1 + R_2 = 5 + 5 = 10\;\Omega$.
Lower branch has $R_3$ and $R_4$ in series: $R_{34} = R_3 + R_4 = 5 + 10 = 15\;\Omega$.

solution: For ground state ($n_1 = 1$), radius $r_1 = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\text{ m}$. For third excited state ($n_2 = 4$), radius $r_2 = 8.48 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}$. text: A circular disk of radius $R$ meter and mass $M\text{ kg}$ is rotating around the axis perpendicular to the disk. An external torque is applied to the disk such that $\theta(t) = 5t^2 - 8t$, where $\theta(t)$ is the angular position of the rotating disc as a function of time $t$. How much power is delivered by the applied torque, when $t = 2\text{s}$?
solution:
$\theta = 5t^2 - 8t$
$\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt} = 10t - 8$
$\alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt} = 10$
$\therefore p = \tau \omega$
$= (I\alpha) \omega$
$= \left(\frac{MR^2}{2}\right) \alpha \omega$
$= \left(\frac{MR^2}{2}\right) (10)(10t - 8)$
Put $t = 2$
$p = 60\text{ MR}^2$

text: The amount of work done to break a big water drop of radius 'R' into 27 small drops of equal radius is $10\text{ J}$. The work done required to break the same big drop into 64 small drops of equal radius will be :-
solution:
$W = \Delta U = S \Delta A$
For one drop to n drops:
$\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = n \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3$
$r = \frac{R}{n^{1/3}}$
So $W = S(n 4 \pi r^2 - 4 \pi R^2) = S 4 \pi R^2 \left( n^{1/3} - 1 \right)$
For one drop to 27 drops:
$W = S 4 \pi R^2 \left( 27^{1/3} - 1 \right) = 10 \dots (i)$
For one drop to 64 drops:
$W' = S 4 \pi R^2 \left( 64^{1/3} - 1 \right) \dots (ii)$
$(ii)/(i) \implies \frac{W'}{W} = \frac{4-1}{3-1} = \frac{3}{2}$
$W' = \frac{3}{2} W = 15\text{ J}$

text: In the first configuration (1) as shown in the figure, four identical charges ($q_0$) are kept at the corners A, B, C and D of square of side length '$a$'. In the second configuration (2), the same charges are shifted to mid points G, E, H and F, of the square, If $K = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$, the difference between the potential energies of configuration (2) and (1) is given by :
solution:
Potential energy of configuration (1) with 4 charges at the corners of a square of side $a$:
$$U_1 = K \sum \frac{q_i q_j}{r_{ij}} = K q_0^2 \left( \frac{4}{a} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}a} \right) = \frac{K q_0^2}{a} \left( 4 + \sqrt{2} \right)$$

Potential energy of configuration (2) with 4 charges at the midpoints of the sides of the square:
Distance between adjacent midpoints is $\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ and opposite midpoints is $a$.
$$U_2 = K q_0^2 \left( \frac{4}{\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}} + \frac{2}{a} \right) = \frac{K q_0^2}{a} \left( 4\sqrt{2} + 2 \right)$$

Difference in potential energy:
$$U_2 - U_1 = \frac{K q_0^2}{a} \left[ (4\sqrt{2} + 2) - (4 + \sqrt{2}) \right] = \frac{K q_0^2}{a} (3\sqrt{2} - 2)$$

text: A point charge $+q$ is placed at the origin. A second point charge $+9q$ is placed at $(d, 0, 0)$ in Cartesian coordinate system. The point in between them where the electric field vanishes is :
solution:
Let the point where electric field vanishes be at a distance $x$ from the origin along the x-axis.
Electric field due to $+q$ equals electric field due to $+9q$ at distance $(d-x)$:
$$\frac{kq}{x^2} = \frac{9kq}{(d-x)^2}$$
$$\frac{1}{x} = \frac{3}{d-x}$$
$$d - x = 3x \implies 4x = d \implies x = \frac{d}{4}$$
So the coordinate is $(\frac{d}{4}, 0, 0)$.

text: Given a charge q, current I and permeability of vacuum $\mu_0$. Which of the following quantity has the dimension of momentum?
solution:
$Q = AT$
$I = A$

$P = Q^x \mu_0^y I^z = [AT]^x [\text{MLT}^{-2}\text{A}^{-2}]^y [A]^z$
$\text{MLT}^{-1} = \text{M}^y \text{L}^y \text{T}^{x-2y} \text{A}^{-2y+z+x}$
Now; $y = 1$
$x - 2y = -1$
$-2y + z = 0$
$\therefore x = y = z = 1$

Which of the following curves possibly represent one-dimensional motion of a particle?

(C) Velocity vs time (circle centered at origin)
(D) Total distance vs time (curve increasing with time)

solution:

$\phi = kt + C$, it can be 1D motion, e.g., $x = A\sin(\phi)$ (SHM).

text: A parallel plate capacitor is filled equally (half) with two dielectrics of dielectric constant $\varepsilon_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$, as shown in figures. The distance between the plates is $d$ and area of each plate is $A$. If capacitance in first configuration and second configuration are $C_1$ and $C_2$ respectively, then $\frac{C_1}{C_2}$ is :
solution:
Area of plate is $A$.
For the first configuration (series combination of two capacitors of thickness $d/2$):
$C_1 = \frac{C_A C_B}{C_A + C_B}$, where $C_A = \frac{\varepsilon_2 \varepsilon_0 A}{d/2} = \frac{2\varepsilon_2 \varepsilon_0 A}{d}$ and $C_B = \frac{\varepsilon_1 \varepsilon_0 A}{d/2} = \frac{2\varepsilon_1 \varepsilon_0 A}{d}$.
Thus, $C_1 = \frac{2\varepsilon_1 \varepsilon_2 \varepsilon_0 A}{d(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)}$.
For the second configuration (parallel combination of two capacitors of area $A/2$):
$C_2 = \frac{\varepsilon_1 \varepsilon_0 (A/2)}{d} + \frac{\varepsilon_2 \varepsilon_0 (A/2)}{d} = \frac{(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\varepsilon_0 A}{2d}$.
Taking the ratio $\frac{C_1}{C_2}$:
$\frac{C_1}{C_2} = \frac{4\varepsilon_1 \varepsilon_2}{(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)^2}$.

Magnetic field $B = \frac{M T^{-2}}{A L T^{-1}}$
So $\left[\frac{E}{B}\right] = \frac{M L^{-3} A^{-1}}{M T^{-2} A^{-1}} = L T^{-1}$
Comparing with $M^P L^Q T^R A^S$, we get $P=0, Q=1, R=-1, S=0$. Thus $Q=1, R=-1$.

text: There are two vessels filled with an ideal gas where volume of one is double the volume of other. The large vessel contains the gas at $8\text{ kPa}$ at $1000\text{ K}$ while the smaller vessel contains the gas at $7\text{ kPa}$ at $500\text{ K}$. If the vessels are connected to each other by a thin tube allowing the gas to flow and the temperature of both vessels is maintained at $600\text{ K}$, at steady state the pressure in the vessels will be (in $\text{kPa}$).
solution:
Initial state: $P_1, V_1, T_1$ and $P_2, V_2, T_2$. Let $V_2 = V$, so $V_1 = 2V$.
Using conservation of mass (number of moles):
$n_1 + n_2 = n_f$
$\frac{P_1 V_1}{R T_1} + \frac{P_2 V_2}{R T_2} = \frac{P_f V_f}{R T_f}$
$\frac{8 \times 2V}{R \times 1000} + \frac{7 \times V}{R \times 500} = \frac{P_f (3V)}{R \times 600}$
$\frac{16}{1000} + \frac{14}{1000} = \frac{P_f}{R \times 200}$
$\frac{30}{1000} = \frac{P_f}{200}$
$P_f = 6\text{ kPa}$

subject: Physics
text: A lens having refractive index $1.6$ has focal length of $12 \text{ cm}$, when it is in air. Find the focal length of the lens when it is placed in water. (Take refractive index of water as $1.28$)
solution:
As we know,
$\frac{1}{f} = \left[\frac{\mu_L}{\mu_m} - 1\right] \left[\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right]$
For air $\mu_m = 1$
$\frac{1}{12} = [1.6 - 1] \left[\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right] \implies \frac{1}{12} = \frac{6}{10} \left[\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right]$
$\left[\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right] = \frac{10}{72}$
For water:
$\frac{1}{f} = \left[\frac{1.6}{1.28} - 1\right] \left[\frac{10}{72}\right] = \frac{32}{128} \times \frac{10}{72} = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{10}{72}$
$f = 28.8 \text{ cm} = 288 \text{ mm}$

Match the List-I with List-II

A. Pressure varies inversely with volume of an ideal gas.
B. Heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work.

D. No work is done on or by a gas

II. Isochoric process
III. Isothermal process

subject: Physics
text: A solid sphere and a hollow sphere of the same mass and of same radius are rolled on an inclined plane. Let the time taken to reach the bottom by the solid sphere and the hollow sphere be $t_1$ and $t_2$, respectively, then
solution: Time taken to reach the bottom is $t = \sqrt{\frac{2l}{a_{\text{cm}}}}$, where acceleration $a_{\text{cm}} = \frac{g \sin\theta}{1 + \frac{I_{\text{cm}}}{MR^2}}$. For solid sphere, $I_{\text{cm}} = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$, so $a_1 = \frac{5g \sin\theta}{7}$. For hollow sphere, $I_{\text{cm}} = \frac{2}{3}MR^2$, so $a_2 = \frac{3g \sin\theta}{5}$. Since $a_1 > a_2$, the time taken is inversely proportional to acceleration, hence $t_1 < t_2$.

subject: Physics
text: Consider a long straight wire of a circular cross-section (radius a) carrying a steady current $I$. The current is uniformly distributed across this cross-section. The distances from the centre of the wire's cross-section at which the magnetic field [inside the wire, outside the wire] is half of the maximum possible magnetic field, any where due to the wire, will be
solution:
Maximum possible magnetic field is at the surface:
$$B_{\text{max}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}$|
$$\frac{B_{\text{max}}}{2} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}$|
It can be obtained inside as well as outside the wire.
For inside ($r < a$):
$$\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a} = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2} \Rightarrow r = \frac{a}{2}$|
For outside ($r > a$):
$$\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \Rightarrow r = 2a$
Correct answer $\left[\frac{a}{2}, 2a\right]$

subject: Physics
text: Two concave refracting surfaces of equal radii of curvature and refractive index $1.5$ face each other in air as shown in figure. A point object $\text{O}$ is placed midway, between $\text{P}$ and $\text{B}$. The separation between the images of $\text{O}$, formed by each refracting surface is :
solution:
For surface B:
$$\frac{\mu_2}{v} - \frac{\mu_1}{u} = \frac{\mu_2 - \mu_1}{R}$$
$$\frac{1.5}{V} + \frac{1}{R} = \frac{0.5}{-R}$$
$$\frac{1.5}{V} = -\frac{1}{2R} - \frac{2}{R} = \frac{-5}{2R} \Rightarrow V_B = -0.6R$$

For surface A:
$$\frac{1.5}{V} + \frac{2}{3R} = \frac{0.5}{-R}$$
$$\frac{1.5}{V} = -\frac{1}{2R} - \frac{2}{3R} = -\frac{7}{6R} \Rightarrow V_A = -\frac{9}{7}R$$

Distance between images:
$$= 2R - \left(0.6R + \frac{9}{7}R\right) = 0.114R$$

and $x_2 = 2\sqrt{7}\sin\left(5t + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\text{ cm}$
where $x$ is displacement and $t$ is time in seconds. The maximum acceleration of the particle is $x \times 10^{-2}\text{ ms}^{-2}$. The value of $x$ is :
solution: Given $x_1 = \sqrt{7}\sin 5t$ and $x_2 = 2\sqrt{7}\sin\left(5t + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)$. From phasor addition with angle $60^{\circ}$ between them, the amplitude of resultant SHM is $A = 7$. Angular frequency $\omega = 5\text{ rad/s}$. Maximum acceleration $a_{\text{max}} = A\omega^2 = 7 \times (5)^2 = 175\text{ cm/sec}^2 = 175 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m/sec}^2$. Thus, the value of $x$ is $175$.

text: A monochromatic light of frequency $5 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}$ travelling through air, is incident on a medium of refractive index '2'. Wavelength of the refracted light will be :
solution:

Speed of light in vacuum $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$.
$\lambda_{\text{medium}} = \frac{\lambda_{\text{vacuum}}}{\mu} = \frac{c}{f \mu}$
$\lambda_{\text{medium}} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{2 \times 5 \times 10^{14}} = 0.3 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m} = 300\text{ nm}$.

text: When an object is placed $40\text{ cm}$ away from a spherical mirror an image of magnification $\frac{1}{2}$ is produced. To obtain an image with magnification of $\frac{1}{3}$, the object is to be moved :

text: An object is kept at rest at a distance of $3R$ above the earth's surface where $R$ is earth's radius. The minimum speed with which it must be projected so that it does not return to earth is : (Assume $M = \text{mass of earth, } G = \text{Universal gravitational constant}$)
solution:
Using conservation of mechanical energy:
$E_i = E_f$
$-\frac{GM m}{R + 3R} + \frac{1}{2}m v^2 = 0$
$\frac{1}{2}m v^2 = \frac{GM m}{4R}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{2R}}$

text: An ac current is represented as $i = 5\sqrt{2} + 10\cos\left(650\pi t + \frac{\pi}{6}\right) \text{ Amp}$. The r.m.s value of the current is:

$\langle i^2 \rangle = 50 + \frac{100}{2} + 0 = 100$
$\langle i^2 \rangle = 100 \implies \langle i \rangle_{\text{rms}} = 10 \text{ Amp}$

text: A mirror is used to produce an image with magnification of $\frac{1}{4}$. If the distance between object and its image is $40\text{ cm}$, then the focal length of the mirror is $\dots\dots$.
solution:
$m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\left(\frac{v}{-u}\right) = \frac{v}{u}$
$\frac{1}{4} = \frac{v}{u} \Rightarrow u = 4v$
$v + u = 40$
$5v = 40 \Rightarrow v = 8\text{ cm}, u = 32\text{ cm}$
$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$
$\frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{32} = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow \frac{4 - 1}{32} = \frac{1}{f} \Rightarrow f = \frac{32}{3} = 10.7\text{ cm}$

subject: Physics
text: Two metal spheres of radius $R$ and $3R$ have same surface charge density $\sigma$. If they are brought in contact and then separated, the surface charge density on smaller and bigger sphere becomes $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, respectively. The ratio $\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2}$ is.
solution: For conducting sphere, $V = \frac{\sigma r}{\varepsilon_0}$. After contact, $V_1 = V_2$. Therefore, $\sigma_1 r_1 = \sigma_2 r_2 \implies \frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2} = \frac{r_2}{r_1} = \frac{3R}{R} = 3$.

subject: Physics
text:
Consider a moving coil galvanometer (MCG) :

A : The torsional constant in moving coil galvanometer has dimensions $[ML^2T^{-2}]$
B : Increasing the current sensitivity may not necessarily increase the voltage sensitivity.
C : If we increase number of turns (N) to its double ($2N$), then the voltage sensitivity doubles.
D : MCG can be converted into an ammeter by introducing a shunt resistance of large value in parallel with galvanometer.
E : Current sensitivity of MCG depends inversely on number of turns of coil.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
solution:
(A) $\tau = C\theta \Rightarrow [ML^2T^{-2}] = [C][1]$, so A is correct.

(B) Voltage sensitivity $\text{V.S.} = \frac{\theta}{I} \cdot \frac{1}{R} = \frac{\text{BNA}}{\text{RC}}$. Increasing current sensitivity (C.S. = $\frac{\text{BNA}}{C}$) doesn't necessarily increase voltage sensitivity since it also depends on resistance $R$ and torsional constant $C$. So B is correct.

(C) $\text{V.S.} \propto \frac{\text{NAB}}{\text{CR}}$, if $N$ increases, resistance $R$ may also change ($R \propto N$), so voltage sensitivity may not double.

(D) False, an ammeter requires a *small* shunt resistance in parallel.

(E) Current sensitivity $\text{C.S.} = \frac{\text{NAB}}{C}$, which depends *directly* on the number of turns, not inversely.

subject: Physics
text: If a satellite orbiting the Earth is 9 times closer to the Earth than the Moon, what is the time period of rotation of the satellite? Given rotational time period of Moon $= 27$ days and gravitational attraction between the satellite and the moon is neglected.
solution:
$T^2 \propto R^3$
$$\left(\frac{T_m}{T_s}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{R}{R/9}\right)^3$$
$$\frac{T_m}{T_s} = (3)^3$$
$$\Rightarrow T_s = \left(\frac{27}{27}\right) = 1 \text{ day}$$

subject: Physics
text: A car of mass '$m$' moves on a banked road having radius '$r$' and banking angle $\theta$. To avoid slipping from banked road, the maximum permissible speed of the car is $v_0$. The coefficient of friction $\mu$ between the wheels of the car and the banked road is :-
solution:
For maximum speed on a banked road with friction:
$$N \sin\theta + f \cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{R}$$
$$N \cos\theta - f \sin\theta = mg$$
Dividing and substituting $f = \mu N$:
$$\frac{\sin\theta + \mu \cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \mu \sin\theta} = \frac{v^2}{Rg}$$
$$Rg\tan\theta + \mu Rg = v^2 - v^2\mu\tan\theta$$
$$\mu = \frac{v^2 - Rg\tan\theta}{Rg + v^2\tan\theta}$$

text: Which of the following figure represents the relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit temperatures?

This represents a straight line with a positive slope ($\frac{5}{9}$) and a negative intercept on the C-axis (when $F=0$, $C = -17.78^{\circ}\text{C}$). subject: Physics
text: A bead of mass '$m$' slides without friction on the wall of a vertical circular hoop of radius '$R$' as shown in figure. The bead moves under the combined action of gravity and a massless spring ($k$) attached to the bottom of the hoop. The equilibrium length of the spring is '$R$'. If the bead is released from top of the hoop with (negligible) zero initial speed, velocity of bead, when the length of spring becomes '$R$', would be (spring constant is '$k$', $g$ is acceleration due to gravity)
solution:
By Work Energy Theorem:
$$\Delta W_{\text{all}} = \Delta K$$
$$Mg(R + R\cos 60^{\circ}) + \frac{1}{2}k(R^2 - 0^2) = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$
$$Mg \frac{3R}{2} + \frac{KR^2}{2} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$
$$V = \sqrt{3gR + \frac{KR^2}{m}}$$

subject: Physics
text: A bar magnet has total length $2l = 20$ units and the field point P is at a distance $d = 10$ units from the centre of the magnet. If the relative uncertainty of length measurement is $1\%$, then uncertainty of the magnetic field at point P is :
solution: Method-1 : Without considering uncertainty in $\ell$. $B = \frac{\mu_0 m}{4\pi r^3}$, $B \propto \frac{1}{r^3}$, $\frac{\Delta B}{B} = 3 \times \left(\frac{\Delta r}{r}\right)$. $\%$ uncertainty in $B = 3\%$. Method-2 : With considering uncertainty in $\ell$. $B \propto \frac{1}{r^3}$, $\frac{\Delta B}{B} = \frac{\Delta \ell}{\ell} + 3 \times \left(\frac{\Delta r}{r}\right) = 1 + 3 \times 1 = 4\%$. $\%$ uncertainty in $B = 4\%$. (Note: Official answer key has a typo 'Ans. (2,3)' but the step-by-step solution derives 4% which corresponds to option (2)).

subject: Physics
text: As shown below, bob A of a pendulum having massless string of length '$R$' is released from $60^\circ$ to the vertical. It hits another bob B of half the mass that is at rest on a friction less table in the centre. Assuming elastic collision, the magnitude of the velocity of bob A after the collision will be (take g as acceleration due to gravity)
solution:
Velocity of A just before hitting ($u$):
$$u = \sqrt{2g \frac{R}{2}} = \sqrt{gR}$|
Just after collision, let velocity of A and B be $v_1$ and $v_2$ respectively.
By conservation of momentum (COM):
$$mu = mv_1 + \frac{m}{2}v_2$$
$$2v_1 + v_2 = 2u \quad \text{--- (i)}$$
Coefficient of restitution for elastic collision ($e = 1$):
$$1 = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u}$|
$$\Rightarrow v_2 - v_1 = u \quad \text{--- (ii)}$|
From (i) - (ii):
$$3v_1 = u \Rightarrow v_1 = \frac{u}{3} = \frac{1}{3}\sqrt{gR}$$

subject: Physics
text: Two bodies A and B of equal mass are suspended from two massless springs of spring constant $k_1$ and $k_2$, respectively. If the bodies oscillate vertically such that their amplitudes are equal, the ratio of the maximum velocity of A to the maximum velocity of B is
solution:
Maximum velocity $V = A\omega$. Given amplitudes are equal ($A_1 = A_2$).
$$\frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{A_1\omega_1}{A_2\omega_2} = \frac{\omega_1}{\omega_2} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{k_1}{m}}}{\sqrt{\frac{k_2}{m}}} = \sqrt{\frac{k_1}{k_2}}$$

text:
The relationship between the magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$) and the magnetic permeability ($\mu$) is given by :

solution: We know that $\mu_r = 1 + \chi \Rightarrow \chi = \mu_r - 1$. Also, $\mu = \mu_0 \mu_r \Rightarrow \mu_r = \frac{\mu}{\mu_0}$. Therefore, $\chi = \left(\frac{\mu}{\mu_0} - 1\right)$.

text: Consider two blocks A and B of masses $m_1 = 10\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 5\text{ kg}$ that are placed on a frictionless table. The block A moves with a constant speed $v = 3\text{ m/s}$ towards the block B kept at rest. A spring with spring constant $k = 3000\text{ N/m}$ is attached with the block B as shown in the figure. After the collision, suppose that the blocks A and B, along with the spring in constant compression state, move together, then the compression in the spring is, (Neglect the mass of the spring)

text: Three parallel plate capacitors $C_1$, $C_2$ and $C_3$ each of capacitance $5\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ are connected as shown in figure. text: A closed organ and an open organ tube filled by two different gases having same bulk modulus but different densities $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ respectively. The frequency of $9^{\text{th}}$ harmonic of closed tube is identical with $4^{\text{th}}$ harmonic of open tube. If the length of the closed tube is $10\text{ cm}$ and the density ratio of the gases is $\rho_1 : \rho_2 = 1 : 16$, then the length of the open tube is :
solution:
$9^{\text{th}}$ harmonic of closed pipe $= \frac{9V_1}{4\ell_1}$

$4^{\text{th}}$ harmonic of open pipe $= \frac{2V_2}{\ell_2}$

$\therefore \frac{9V_1}{4\ell_1} = \frac{2V_2}{\ell_2}$

$\therefore \frac{9}{4\ell_1} \sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho_1}} = \frac{2}{\ell_2} \sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho_2}} \Rightarrow \frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1} = \frac{8}{9} \sqrt{\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}}$

$\ell_2 = \ell_1 \times \frac{8}{9} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{20}{9}\text{ cm}$

text: Two point charges $-4\ \mu\text{c}$ and $4\ \mu\text{c}$, constituting an electric dipole, are placed at $(-9, 0, 0)\text{ cm}$ and $(9, 0, 0)\text{ cm}$ in a uniform electric field of strength $10^4\text{ NC}^{-1}$. The work done on the dipole in rotating it from the equilibrium through $180^\circ$ is :
solution:
$U = -PE \cos\theta$
$W_{\text{ext}} = \Delta U = U_f - U_i = -PE \cos 180^\circ + PE \cos 0^\circ$
$W_{\text{ext}} = 2PE$
$= 2 \times (4 \times 10^{-6}) (18) \times 10^4$
$= 144 \times 10^{-2}$
$= 14.4\text{ mJ}$

subject: Physics
text: A uniform solid cylinder of mass '$m$' and radius '$r$' rolls along an inclined rough plane of inclination $45^\circ$. If it starts to roll from rest from the top of the plane then the linear acceleration of the cylinder axis will be :-
solution:
Acceleration for rolling down an inclined plane:
$$a = \frac{g \sin\theta}{1 + \frac{I}{mR^2}}$$
For a solid cylinder, $I = \frac{1}{2}mR^2$, and $\theta = 45^\circ$:
$$a = \frac{g \sin 45^\circ}{1 + \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\frac{g}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} = \frac{2g}{3\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}g}{3}$$

text: Earth has mass 8 times and radius 2 times that of a planet. If the escape velocity from the earth is $11.2 \text{ km/s}$, the escape velocity in $\text{km/s}$ from the planet will be :
solution:
$V_{\text{escape}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}$
$$\frac{(V_{\text{escape}})_{\text{Planet}}}{(V_{\text{escape}})_{\text{Earth}}} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{M_{\text{P}}}{M_{\text{E}}}\right) \times \left(\frac{R_{\text{E}}}{R_{\text{P}}}\right)} = \frac{1}{2}$$
$$(V_{\text{escape}})_{\text{Planet}} = \frac{1}{2}(V_{\text{escape}})_{\text{Earth}} = 5.6 \text{ km/s}$$

text:
Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : 
Three identical spheres of same mass undergo one dimensional motion as shown in figure with initial velocities $v_A = 5	ext{ m/s}$, $v_B = 2	ext{ m/s}$, $v_C = 4	ext{ m/s}$ If we wait sufficiently long for elastic collision to happen, then $v_A = 4	ext{ m/s}$, $v_B = 2	ext{ m/s}$, $v_C = 5	ext{ m/s}$ will be the final velocities.
Reason (R) : In an elastic collision between identical masses, two objects exchange their velocities.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.1: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
options.3: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

solution:
In elastic collision for same mass, velocities interchange.
For A and B: $v'_A = 2	ext{ m/s}$, $v'_B = 5	ext{ m/s}$
For B and C: $v''_B = 4	ext{ m/s}$, $v'_C = 5	ext{ m/s}$
Final velocities: $v'_A = 2	ext{ m/s}$, $v''_B = 4	ext{ m/s}$, $v'_C = 5	ext{ m/s}$.
Thus, Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is true.

text: A piston of mass $M$ is hung from a massless spring whose restoring force law goes as $F = -kx^3$, where $k$ is the spring constant of appropriate dimension. The piston separates the vertical chamber into two parts, where the bottom part is filled with '$n$' moles of an ideal gas. An external work is done on the gas isothermally (at a constant temperature $T$) with the help of a heating filament (with negligible volume) mounted in lower part of the chamber, so that the piston goes up from a height $L_0$ to $L_1$, the total energy delivered by the filament is (Assume spring to be in its natural length before heating)
solution:
Using WET (Work-Energy Theorem):
Total energy supplied = gravitational potential energy + spring potential energy + work done by gas
$$\text{Total energy} = Mg(L_1 - L_0) + \int_{L_0}^{L_1} kx^3 dx + nRT \ln\left(\frac{L_1}{L_0}\right)$$$\text{W}_{ext} = \frac{k}{4}(L_1^4 - L_0^4) + Mg(L_1 - L_0) + nRT \ln\left(\frac{L_1}{L_0}\right)$

A particle is projected with velocity $u$ so that its horizontal range is three times the maximum height attained by it. The horizontal range of the projectile is given as $\frac{n u^2}{25g}$, where value of $n$ is :

solution:
Given $\text{Range} = 3 H_{\text{max}}$
$\frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g} = \frac{3 u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$
$2 \sin \theta \cos \theta = \frac{3}{2} \sin^2 \theta$
$\tan \theta = \frac{4}{3} \Rightarrow \theta = 53^{\circ}$
$R = \frac{u^2 \left(2 \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{4}{5}\right)}{g} = \frac{24 u^2}{25g}$
Thus, $n = 24$.

text:
In the following circuit, the reading of the ammeter will be (Take Zener breakdown voltage $= 4\text{ V}$)

![Circuit Diagram](https://example.com/circuit.png)
solution:
First, let's find the voltage across the $400\Omega$ resistor assuming no Zener diode is present or to check the potential divider voltage:
$$V_1 = \frac{400}{100 + 400} \times 12\text{ V} = \frac{4}{5} \times 12 = \frac{48}{5}\text{ V} = 9.6\text{ V}$$
Here, $V_1 > V_z$ (where $V_z = 4\text{ V}$ is the Zener Voltage).
So, Zener breakdown will take place.
Thus, the voltage across the $400\Omega$ resistor will be clamped at $4\text{ V}$.
The current through the ammeter (which is in series with the $400\Omega$ resistor) is:
$$I = \frac{4\text{ V}}{400\Omega} = \frac{1}{100}\text{ A} = 10\text{ mA}$$

subject: Physics
text: A uniform circular disc of radius 'R' and mass 'M' is rotating about an axis perpendicular to its plane and passing through its centre. A small circular part of radius $R/2$ is removed from the original disc as shown in the figure. Find the moment of inertia of the remaining part of the original disc about the axis as given above.
solution:
Let the original mass of the disc be $M$ and radius $R$. The surface mass density is $\sigma = \frac{M}{\pi R^2}$.

The radius of the removed portion is $r = R/2$, and its mass is $m' = \sigma \pi \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{M}{4}$.
The distance of the centre of the removed portion from the axis of rotation is $d = R/2$.

Moment of inertia of the removed portion about the central axis:
$I_{\text{removed}} = \frac{1}{2} m' r^2 + m' d^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{M}{4}\right) \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{M}{4}\right) \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^2$
$= \frac{MR^2}{32} + \frac{MR^2}{16} = \frac{3}{32} MR^2$

Moment of inertia of the original disc: $I_{\text{original}} = \frac{1}{2} MR^2 = \frac{16}{32} MR^2$

Moment of inertia of the remaining part:
$I_{\text{remaining}} = I_{\text{original}} - I_{\text{removed}} = \frac{16}{32} MR^2 - \frac{3}{32} MR^2 = \frac{13}{32} MR^2$

text:
Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : Knowing initial position $x_0$ and initial momentum $p_0$ is enough to determine the position and momentum at any time t for a simple harmonic motion with a given angular frequency $\omega$.
Reason (R) : The amplitude and phase can be expressed in terms of $x_0$ an $p_0$.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.1: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
options.4: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

solution:
$x = A \sin(\omega t + \phi)$
$x_0 = A \sin\phi \quad \dots(1)$
$p = m\omega \cos(\omega t + \phi)$
$p_0 = m\omega \cos\phi \quad \dots(2)$
$(2)/(1) \Rightarrow \tan\phi = \left(\frac{x_0}{p_0}\right) m\omega$
$\sin\phi = \frac{x_0 m \omega}{\sqrt{(m \omega x_0)^2 + p_0^2}}$
From $(1)$, $A = \frac{x_0}{\sin\phi} = \frac{\sqrt{(m\omega x_0)^2 + p_0^2}}{m\omega}$
This means we can explain assertion with the given reason.

$F =  rac{dp}{dt} [p = mv]$

text: In an adiabatic process, which of the following statements is true ?

options.2: Work done by the gas equals the increase in internal energy
options.3: The molar heat capacity is zero
options.4: The internal energy of the gas decreases as the temperature increases

solution:
For adiabatic process, $dQ = 0$
$\therefore \text{Molar heat capacity} = 0$
$\because dQ = 0 \implies dU = -dW$
Also $dU = \frac{f}{2}nRdT$

text:
A gas is kept in a container having walls which are thermally non-conducting. Initially the gas has a volume of $800\text{ cm}^3$ and temperature $27^{\circ}\text{C}$. The change in temperature when the gas is adiabatically compressed to $200\text{ cm}^3$ is :
(Take $\gamma = 1.5$ : $\gamma$ is the ratio of specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume)
solution:
$V_1 = 800\text{ cm}^3$, $V_2 = 200\text{ cm}^3$
$T_1 = 27^{\circ}\text{C} = 300\text{ K}$
For adiabatic process:
$TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const.}$
$(300)(800)^{1.5-1} = T_2(200)^{1.5-1}$
$T_2 = 300\left[\frac{800}{200}\right]^{0.5} = 300 \times (2^2)^{1/2}$
$T_2 = 600\text{ K}$
Change in temperature $\Delta T = 600 - 300 = 300\text{ K}$

$v_{\text{T}} = \frac{2}{9} \frac{(ho_0 - ho_{\ell}) r^2 g}{\eta}$

text: Two projectiles are fired from ground with same initial speeds from same point at angles $(45^\circ + \alpha)$ and $(45^\circ - \alpha)$ with horizontal direction. The ratio of their times of flights is
solution:
Given angles of projection: $\theta_1 = 45^\circ + \alpha$ and $\theta_2 = 45^\circ - \alpha$.
Time of flight is given by $T = \frac{2v \sin\theta}{g}$.
$$\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{\sin(45^\circ + \alpha)}{\sin(45^\circ - \alpha)}$$$
Using the sine expansion:
$$\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\alpha + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\alpha}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\alpha - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\alpha}$$
Dividing numerator and denominator by $\cos\alpha$:
$$\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{\cos\alpha + \sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha - \sin\alpha} = \frac{1 + \tan\alpha}{1 - \tan\alpha}$$
